newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Howard rejects compensation for "stolen" Aborigines.
newsitem.headline: Howard rejects compensation for "stolen" Aborigines.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard on Wednesday rejected calls to pay compensation to Aborigines for the forced removal of children from their families during decades of forced assimilation.

"This is asking one generation to accept legal responsibility for the acts of earlier generations," Howard told parliament, resisting an opposition motion for compensation during an emotional debate on Australia's "stolen generation".
"Once a nation begins to go down that path, there is in fact no end," he added.

The parliamentary Labor opposition has joined Aboriginal leaders in calling for compensation for thousands of Aborigines abducted from their parents in a policy described as genocidal in a human rights report issued this week.
The forced assimilation practice only stopped in the 1960s.

Labor opposition leader Kim Beazley had tears in his eyes on Wednesday as he moved for parliament to set up processes for compensation and asked the government to unreservedly apologise for the brutal assimilation policy.

Beazley said the report detailed extraordinary experiences of children taken from their families to be exposed to sexual and physical assault, although he conceded that the current government was not to blame.
"This is a terrible record, a terrible, terrible record," Beazley said, halting sometimes to contain his emotion. "This is not a matter that we can sweep under this table."
The 700-page report on the "stolen generation" called for compensation and a government apology for what it called a policy amounting to genocide under international law.
The report contained a litany of physical and sexual abuse of Aborigines based predominantly on a policy of white racial superiority.
But Howard said that paying compensation for an earlier bad policy would open the floodgates for future claims on any number of policies that later appeared unwise.

"There will be no end to the number of claims that can be made and allegations made that the conduct of an earlier generation, judged at the time to be acceptable by people on both sides of politics in that earlier generation..." he said.
The Liberal-National government used its clear majority in the lower house of parliament to block the compensation motion.
